title: Haemul Pajeon
subtitle: Seafood and spring onion savoury pancake
excerpt: A crisp, golden Korean savoury pancake packed with whole spring onions and mixed seafood. The batter is thin so the filling is the star. Two large pancakes serve 4 and take about 35 minutes in total. Serve with a sharp soy dipping sauce.
sourceNotes: Pajeon has been a feature of Korean cooking for centuries, with regional variations across the peninsula. The Dongnae pajeon from Busan and the haemul pajeon from coastal areas are the best known. These pancakes became widely popular as street food and are now a fixture at Korean restaurants worldwide.

glossaryTerms.definition: Pajeon is a Korean savoury pancake made with a thin batter and whole spring onions laid in the pan. The name comes from pa (spring onion) and jeon (pan-fried item). It is eaten as a snack, a starter, or a side dish, and is particularly associated with rainy days in Korean culture.

Makgeolli is a traditional Korean rice wine with a milky appearance and a slightly sweet, tangy flavour. It has a low alcohol content and is made by fermenting rice with a starter culture. Adding a small amount to pancake batter is a common trick that adds lightness and a subtle flavour complexity.

Cold water is the key to a crisp pancake. Mix the batter only until just combined and keep it cold. Some Korean cooks swap a small amount of water for

content.text: Make the dipping sauce: mix 2 tablespoons soy sauce, the rice vinegar, sesame oil, and gochugaru together in a small bowl. Set aside.
In a bowl, whisk together the flour, eggs, 1 tablespoon soy sauce, and 200ml cold water until just combined. A few lumps are fine. Do not overwork the batter.
Add the seafood to the batter and stir to distribute.
Heat 2 tablespoons of oil in a large frying pan over high heat until shimmering. Lay half the spring onions in the pan in a single layer, running them parallel.
Pour half the batter over the spring onions, spreading it to the edges. Reduce the heat to medium-high and cook for 4 to 5 minutes until the edges are set and golden.

Flip the pancake using a large spatula or by sliding it onto a plate and inverting it back into the pan. Add a little more oil around the edges. Cook for a further 3 to 4 minutes until the second side is golden and crisp.
Slide onto a board, cut into pieces, and serve immediately. Repeat with the remaining batter and spring onions.

items.symptom: The pancake is soft rather than crisp
items.cause: The pan was not hot enough or too little oil was used
items.fix: Use a wide heavy pan on the highest heat. Add enough oil to coat the base generously and let it get very hot before adding the spring onions

items.symptom: The pancake falls apart when flipping
items.cause: The batter was too thin or the first side was not cooked long enough
items.fix: Wait until the edges are clearly set and the top surface looks mostly dry before attempting to flip. Use a wide spatula and move decisively

items.cause: Squid overcooks very quickly and becomes tough if left in the pan too long
items.fix: Cut squid into small pieces and add it to the batter just before cooking. The short frying time is enough to cook it through without toughening it

content.text: Haemul pajeon is strongly associated with rainy days in Korean culture. There is a well-known saying that the sound of rain on a roof is similar to the sound of jeon sizzling in a pan. Koreans often crave these pancakes when it rains. They are sold from street stalls, at traditional markets, and in restaurants that specialise in jeon alongside makgeolli. At home, they are a quick and satisfying midweek meal that uses whatever seafood is available.
